claim: Gao et al. partition published RAG systems into three paradigms - Naive (retrieve-read), Advanced (pre/post-retrieval optimization), and Modular (Search, Memory, Routing, Predict, Task-Adapter modules with adaptive flow).

evidence.quote: we categorize it into three stages: Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and Modular RAG
The Modular RAG framework introduces additional specialized components to enhance retrieval and processing capabilities. The Search module adapts to specific scenarios

applies_when: any 10M-doc design considering adaptive vs single-shot retrieval

claim: Across Naive RAG, retrieval precision/recall failures plus generator over-reliance on retrieved chunks are the two dominant failure modes; both are explicit motivators for Advanced/Modular extensions (rerank, query rewrite, adaptive retrieval).

evidence.quote: Retrieval Challenges. The retrieval phase often struggles with precision and recall, leading to the selection of misaligned or irrelevant chunks, and the missing of crucial information.

applies_when: single-pass retrieval at 10M scale where misses cost faithfulness

claim: Sentence-level chunking at 512 tokens (20-token overlap) maximizes both faithfulness (97.59) and relevancy (97.41) on the lyft_2021 doc QA benchmark; 2048-token chunks collapse faithfulness to 80.37.

evidence.quote: Larger chunks provide more context, enhancing comprehension but increasing process time. Smaller chunks improve retrieval recall and reduce time but may lack sufficient context.

applies_when: doc QA where chunks fed to GPT-3.5/Zephyr-7B with ada-002 embeddings; effect may shift with long-context models

claim: BAAI bge-large-en achieves MRR@10 37.66 and R@10 66.09 on namespace-Pt/msmarco; BAAI LLM-Embedder reaches comparable MRR@10 37.58 / R@10 66.45 at ~1/3 the model size, making it the recommended default in Best-Practices ablations.

evidence.quote: LLM-Embedder [20] achieves comparable results with BAAI/bge-large-en [12], however, the size of the former is three times smaller than that of the latter.

applies_when: English open-domain retrieval; MTEB-style passage matching

claim: HyDE plus hybrid (BM25 + dense) retrieval lifts TREC DL19 nDCG@10 from 50.58 (BM25 alone) to 73.34 but raises per-query latency from 0.07s to 11.16s (LLM-Embedder backbone, Section 3.4 Table 6).
applies_when: latency budget >= ~12s/query or HyDE can be cached/async; otherwise prefer hybrid without HyDE (3.20s) for 72.50 nDCG@10

claim: Of five open-source vector DBs evaluated (Weaviate, Faiss, Chroma, Qdrant, Milvus), only Milvus satisfies all four criteria: multiple index types, billion-scale vectors, hybrid search, and cloud-native deployment (Table 5).

evidence.quote: Our evaluation indicates that Milvus stands out as the most comprehensive solution among the databases evaluated, meeting all the essential criteria and outperforming other open-source options.

applies_when: 10M+ corpus requiring billion-scale headroom and hybrid (dense+sparse) search; subjective rubric, criteria-dependent

claim: Pipelining retrieval with generation via a stale query window (PipeRAG) gives up to 2.6x end-to-end latency speedup over Retro at iso-perplexity, or 0.93 perplexity reduction at iso-latency on the 200B-token C4 database.

evidence.quote: PipeRAG can achieve up to 2.6 $\times$ speedup in latency without compromising perplexity; alternatively, maintaining the same latency allows PipeRAG to reduce perplexity by as much as 0.93 compared to Retro.

applies_when: periodic retrieval architectures (Retro-style) with cross-attention to retrieved chunks; less directly applicable to one-shot RAG over chat LLMs

claim: ANN search exhibits a hard quality-vs-latency Pareto: expanding nprobe in IVF-PQ improves recall but linearly grows scan cost. PipeRAG exploits this by sizing search space to fit under the next-chunk inference latency budget.

evidence.quote: there exists a fundamental trade-off between search quality and latency in ANN search... Expanding the search space would enhance the probability of finding the query vector's true nearest neighbors

applies_when: any IVF/IVF-PQ/HNSW index at scale where p95 latency is bounded

claim: GPT-4 and ChatGPT score 59% and 55% respectively on 3-digit by 3-digit multiplication, indicating compositional reasoning collapses even at small problem sizes; this caps multi-hop RAG accuracy when intermediate computation is required.

evidence.quote: off-the-shelf ChatGPT and GPT4 achieve only 55% and 59% accuracies on this task, respectively

applies_when: multi-hop QA requiring chained numeric/logical reasoning over retrieved facts; for direct lookup the limit is irrelevant

claim: Transformer LLMs reduce multi-step compositional tasks to linearized subgraph matching against training data; OOD examples deeper/wider than training graph fail near-zero even with scratchpad fine-tuning - implication: do not rely on the generator to chain retrieved facts beyond a few hops.

evidence.quote: transformer LLMs solve compositional tasks by reducing multi-step compositional reasoning into linearized subgraph matching, without necessarily developing systematic problem-solving skills.
GPT3 exhibits poor generalization with increasing graph depth and width

applies_when: multi-hop reasoning chains > 3 hops; pushes design toward decomposition + verification (CoVe, Self-RAG) over single-prompt generation

claim: RAGAS reference-free faithfulness metric (|supported statements| / |total statements| extracted from the answer) agrees with human pairwise judgement at 0.95 accuracy on WikiEval - far above GPT Score (0.72) and GPT Ranking (0.54).

evidence.quote: The final faithfulness score, $F$ , is then computed as $F=\frac{|V|}{|S|}$ , where $|V|$ is the number of statements that were supported according to the LLM and $|S|$ is the total number of statements.

applies_when: long-form answers where atomic statement decomposition is feasible; for extractive short answers the metric saturates

claim: RAGAS uses gpt-3.5-turbo-16k as judge for all three metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, context relevance), meaning evaluation cost scales with judge token usage and inherits judge-model biases (note: judge != generator).

evidence.quote: all prompts are evaluated using the gpt-3.5-turbo-16k model, which is available through the OpenAI API

applies_when: production teams must budget judge-LLM cost separately from generator cost; for higher fidelity, upgrade judge to gpt-4 class

claim: Context Relevance measured as fraction of context sentences flagged as crucial by an LLM is the weakest of the three RAGAS metrics (0.70 human agreement), driven by judge LLM struggling on long contexts.

evidence.quote: we observed that ChatGPT often struggles with the task of selecting the sentences from the context that are crucial, especially for longer contexts.

applies_when: long retrieved contexts (>~2k tokens); for shorter contexts agreement is higher

claim: Prepending an LLM-generated 50-100 token chunk-specific context summary to each chunk before embedding reduces top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 35% (5.7% to 3.7%) on Anthropic's internal eval.

evidence.quote: Contextual Embeddings reduced the top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 35% (5.7% → 3.7%).

applies_when: 10M-doc corpora where retrieval recall@20 currently bottlenecked at ~94%; indexing cost is one LLM call per chunk (cacheable)

claim: Combining Contextual Embeddings with Contextual BM25 (hybrid lexical+dense with context-augmented chunks) reduces top-20 retrieval failure rate by 49% (5.7% to 2.9%) over baseline.

evidence.quote: Combining Contextual Embeddings and Contextual BM25 reduced the top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 49% (5.7% → 2.9%).

applies_when: hybrid retrieval is acceptable in the pipeline; ~2x indexing cost vs pure-dense

claim: Stacking a reranker on top of Contextual Embeddings + Contextual BM25 reduces top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 67% (5.7% to 1.9%); reranking provides the single largest delta in the stack.

evidence.quote: Reranked Contextual Embedding and Contextual BM25 reduced the top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 67% (5.7% → 1.9%).

applies_when: latency budget tolerates an extra rerank pass (~100-500ms for top-100 candidates); high faithfulness target

claim: On reasoning-heavy data, Cohere Rerank 3.5 retrieves 81.59% accurate top-results vs BM25 43.53%, Dense 50.64%, Hybrid 48.80%; the rerank delta widens substantially on harder query distributions.

evidence.quote: BM25 43.53% / Dense Embeddings 50.64% / Hybrid Search 48.80% / Cohere Rerank 3 27.91% / Cohere Rerank 3.5 81.59%

applies_when: queries require reasoning over retrieved evidence; vendor-published benchmark, may be cherry-picked

claim: Multilingual nDCG@10: Cohere Rerank 3.5 hits 62.18% vs Dense 53.83%, Hybrid 52.10%, BM25 38.19% across 18 languages.

evidence.quote: BM25 38.19% / Dense Embeddings 53.83% / Hybrid Search 52.10% / Cohere Rerank 3 52.27% / Cohere Rerank 3.5 62.18%

applies_when: multilingual corpus (English-primary + others); 10M-doc scale where reranker per-query cost is affordable

claim: Qdrant payload indexes MUST be created before data ingestion to benefit from filter-aware HNSW edges; creating them post-ingestion requires full HNSW rebuild.

evidence.quote: Payload indexes should be created before ingesting data. Qdrant's filterable HNSW index only benefits from additional filter-aware edges when it is generated after the payload indexes have been created.

applies_when: Qdrant as vector DB; filtered retrieval required (metadata filters); 10M+ vectors where HNSW rebuild is multi-hour

claim: Qdrant strict-mode `unindexed_filtering_retrieve=false` fails queries against unindexed fields at the API boundary, surfacing misconfiguration as errors instead of silent latency spikes.

evidence.quote: To block queries that filter on unindexed fields, enable strict mode and set unindexed_filtering_retrieve to false. Qdrant will then return an error if a search query attempts to filter on an unindexed field. On Qdrant Cloud, these settings are applied to all collections by default.

applies_when: production Qdrant deployments where p95 latency SLO matters

claim: Cohere reference architecture: BM25 retrieves top-100 candidates -> rerank API call returns top-N (3 or 10); the 100-candidate window is the standard rerank input size for production-grade quality.

evidence.quote: We use BM25 lexical search to retrieve the top-100 passages matching the query and then send these 100 passages and the query to our rerank endpoint to get a re-ranked list.

applies_when: two-stage retrieve+rerank pipeline; rerank API charged per (query, candidate) pair so the 100-cap is a cost/quality knob

claim: A 70% pass rate on production-derived evals is more informative than 95% on a static gold benchmark; chasing high pass rates indicates the test set is too easy to expose real failure modes.

evidence.quote: A 70% on meaningful, production-derived evals tells you more than 95% on a benchmark that doesn't reflect your users.

applies_when: production-traffic available for sampling; not applicable to pre-launch systems where synthetic eval is the only option

claim: End-to-end RAG eval lets the generator absorb retriever failures and hide them in green pass-rates; Recall@K < 0.5-0.6 is a strong signal the retriever is the bottleneck, Precision@K < 0.4 signals excessive noise into the generator.

evidence.quote: Recall@K below 0.5–0.6 is a strong signal your retriever is the bottleneck.
Precision@K below 0.4 suggests your retriever is adding too much noise.

applies_when: retriever and generator can be evaluated independently with held-out QA + gold-evidence labels

claim: Custom domain-specific trace-viewing UI yields more eval insights per engineer-hour than generic dashboards (LangSmith, Phoenix, etc.) - the highest-leverage tooling investment for an AI team improving a RAG system.

evidence.quote: The single most impactful investment I've seen AI teams make isn't a fancy evaluation dashboard – it's building a customized interface that lets anyone examine what their AI is actually doing.

applies_when: team has engineering bandwidth to build internal tools; domain-specific context matters (e.g. legal, medical, finance)

claim: For RAG generation eval, do NOT use off-the-shelf LLM-as-judge prompts; the standard process requires error analysis, prompt iteration, labeled examples, and measuring judge TPR/TNR against human annotators before estimates can be trusted.

evidence.quote: Finally, when implementing Jason's Tier 2 and 3 metrics, don't just use prompts off the shelf. The standard LLM-as-judge process requires several steps: error analysis, prompt iteration, creating labeled examples, and measuring your judge's accuracy against human labels.

applies_when: production hallucination targets near-zero; budget for human-annotation calibration phase before judge-LLM scales

claim: Cite-or-refuse contracts: if a retrieved chunk is below a confidence threshold, force refusal instead of generating an unsupported answer; this converts a known failure mode (confident hallucination) into a known refusal that the product layer can handle.

evidence.quote: If retrieval confidence is too low, the assistant refuses instead of guessing. If the user asks for private or internal data, the system refuses early.

applies_when: near-zero hallucination is a hard requirement; product can present a refusal gracefully (chat UI, not search)
